messages.subject: Distribution for modeling a scale
parts:
I have a variable that takes on values in the range 1-4. I was thinking
of modeling this as a beta distribution, but since there are a lot of
cases at the extremes that seems problematic. I'm not sure the beta
function in stan will even accept such inputs and produce estimates. I
could fake it by pulling the values in a bit, but I'm not sure that's a
good idea.

I'd appreciate any suggestions on how to fit such outcomes. I don't
think it's a big deal if the fit doesn't reproduce the detailed features
of the distribution for my purposes, though if this lack of fit leads to
estimation problems that would matter.

"Detailed" features refers to that fact that most of the observations
are exactly integers, and all the values are evenly divisible by 1/3.

My main focus is on how covariates shift the distribution. One approach
might be to treat the outcome as categorical or ordinal, but that seems
likely to create a lot more parameters.

The distribution also kind of looks like a truncated normal if one uses
1 unit size bins.

If you're curious, here's the basic data:

> table(tfat$FrndPartRace)

1 1.33333333333333 1.66666666666667 2
162 55 83 156
2.33333333333333 2.66666666666667 3 3.33333333333333
71 73 93 19
3.66666666666667 4
5 29

Thanks.
Ross

If you're talking about the "Informational Message" reports, those are NOT
errors, they are warnings.

Did you read the part that says

"If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance
matrices, then the sampler is fine,"

and if so, could you let us know how we can make it clearer that
this is just an informational message and not an error?

You're not the only one who's interpreted these messages as errors.
I think part of the confusion is that the embedded message says "error",
whereas we've tried to keep the referencing part clear that it's a warning.

But we want to keep them because if the rejections happen repeatedly,
then it can be a problem for sampling efficiency (up to the point where
if they happen in every step of every iteration the sampler won't move
at all).

I'm also wondering if users are familiar with the notion of Metropolis
rejection or if that's too much MCMC jargon.

- Bob

Andrew answered this one. Transforms affect modes. It's
why maximum likelihood estimates are sensitive to parameterization.

>> Warning messages:
>> 1: In selectChildren(ac, 1) : error 'Interrupted system call' in select

>> I'm not really sure what to make of the interrupted system call
>> messages, which have not occurred in other, similar, calls.Presumably
>> they are coming from R's parallel library and the underlying OS, rather
>> than stan. Perhaps they have something to do with this being a first
>> time experiment in which I ran more threads than physical cores (4),
>> though fewer than the virtual, hyperthreaded, cores.
No idea, but they're not coming from Stan.

>> At any rate, the computation did return 6 full sets of answers. I'm a
>> little suprised n_eff isn't a bit better given the individual chains:

>> I'd expect n_eff to be more like the sum of the individual chain
>> n_eff's, or at least > than the largest single value. Since chain 2 has
>> min n_eff of 31, how can all the chains together have smaller minimum
>> n_eff than chain 2 alone?

That's what you'd get with more tradition n_eff calculations,
but Stan's is more conservative, using both within-chain and
cross-chain measures. You can see the definition in the Stan manual
and in the new edition of Gelman et al.'s Bayesian Data Analysis.

What you'll see is that higher R-hat will cause lower effective sample
sizes. As R-hat goes to 1, the n_eff we calculate will converge to
calculating each chain independently and averaging.

- Bob

That's a good idea. I don't want to be too verbose, but we can
do better than real[1]. I thought the
1 would be confusing. Also, real[2] looks like an array of size
2, not a 2-dimensional array.

I created an issue to fix this in the future:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/529

> My problem was not that I didn't understand the message, but that I
> didn't believe it :) That is, I thought combining arrays and scalars
> must be supported, and so either I had made an error, the system had
> made an error, or I had misunderstood the message.
>
> I think it would be nice if scalars and arrays could be combined. I
> can't think of other examples where they can't (e.g., R, python numeric,
> C++ math libraries other than stan, SAS IML).

Eigen's an example, and it's the C++ math lib we use :-)
You can wrap an array into a matrix or vice-versa, but you can't do
matrix arithmetic on arrays.

The reason we can't just automatically coerce back and forth is
that vectors are either row vectors (1 x K) or column vectors (K x 1),
so there's not an unambiguous way to cast an array without context.

We do allow them to mix in contexts like vectorized probability functions
where the use is unambiguous.

> Does this mean that, unless I have a good reason, I should prefer
> vector[n] x to real x[n]?

There's a chapter in the manual on when to prefer one over the other.
There's really no reason to have 1-dimensional real arrays other than
for generality of notation and similarity to BUGS. There are substantive
differences between 2D arrays and matrices. There are no integer
vectors or matrices, and only arrays can have 3+ dimensions.

- Bob

I took the original 1-4 scale and divided by 5, leaving the range from .2 through .8.  This was to avoid putting a lot of mass at the end points, since the beta doesn't like that (the manual seems  to indicate 0 and 1 are not legal values).  Then I fit a beta model parameterized by mean and "size" (courtesy of wikipedia) where the regression model applied only to the mean.  So there was a 2nd beta parameter, but it was just a single parameter rather than a fuller model.  Finally, when simulating I pull values outside of [1, 4] to the endpoints, which gives me a bit of a pile up at the end points, just like the original data.

Small syntax question: I didn't declare some variables in the model block (I just noticed it); is that a problem (see below)?

Here's the code:
data {
   int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents
   int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates
   int<lower=0> NSD;  // number of classes of beta for sd
   int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J];  // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
   int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of seeds
   int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
   matrix[N, J] x;  // covariates
   vector<lower=1,upper=4>[N] y;  // outcome
}
transformed data {
   vector<lower=0,upper=1>[N] z;
   z <- y/5.0;
}
parameters {
    vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
    vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
    real<lower=0> nu; // 'size' parameter
    real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;
    real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[J] beta;
    vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
    for(ir in 1:J) {
       beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
    }
    alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma_alpha;
}
model {
    vector[N] mu;
    vector[N] parm1;
    vector[N] parm2;
    nu ~ cauchy(0, 5); //maybe it should start above 0

    }
    parm1 <- mu*nu;
    parm2 <- (1-mu)*nu;
    z ~ beta(parm1, parm2);
}

I've been getting more of these selectChildren warnings and looked into it.
Apparently they require all of
1) using R (specifically the parallel library mclapply)
2) using Rmpi
3) using an old version of openmpi.

See
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14149361/rmpi-mclapply-in-selectchildrenac-1-error-interrupted-system-call-in-s
for details (and the link there to the openmpi list).

Apparently loading the Rmpi library resets SIGCHLD handling (or did with
older open mpi's) which produces the warnings.

They appear harmless. And, to repeat, r/stan is a bystander to this
infelicity, not a cause.

Ross Boylan
